The Singular Value Decomposition has a rich history spanning over 150 years, with contributions from Beltrami, Jordan, Eckart & Young, Lanczos, and many others. Stewart’s 1993 overview tells this story well. Today SVD is everywhere: dimensionality reduction, recommender systems, numerical linear algebra, signal processing.

For most practitioners, SVD is a single line: u, s, v = torch.linalg.svd(A). The factorization \(A = U\Sigma V^T\) is derived by finding eigenvectors of \(A^T A\) and \(AA^T\), recognizing they share the same nonzero eigenvalues, and relating the two bases through the singular values. But there is another formulation: derive SVD from a variational principle, finding unit vectors \(u\) and \(v\) that maximize their coupling \(u^T A v\). This is not merely an alternative derivation. It is the entry point to generalizations that the factorization view obscures.

In 2016, Johan Suykens, the creator of LS-SVM, showed in a paper named “SVD revisited: A new variational principle, compatible feature maps and nonlinear extensions” that this variational characterization fits naturally within the Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LS-SVM) framework. The payoff: SVD becomes kernelizable, with asymmetric kernels, two distinct feature maps, and out-of-sample extensions. More recently, this kernel SVD framework has been connected to the attention mechanism in transformers, offering both theoretical insight and practical efficiency gains.

This post develops that foundation. We start with Gilbert Strang’s geometric view of SVD, then move to the classical variational formulation, and finally to Suykens’ reformulation. Part 2 will show how this leads to Primal-Attention.

The Geometry of SVD

Linear Algebra Prerequisites

This post assumes familiarity with eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix factorizations. If you need a refresher:

  • For intuition: Grant Sanderson’s Essence of Linear Algebra builds geometric understanding from first principles

  • For depth: Gilbert Strang’s MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra remains the gold standard for rigorous yet accessible treatment

Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Square Matrix

For a square matrix, eigenvalues and eigenvectors capture its essence. An eigenvector \(v\) satisfies \(Av = \lambda v\): the matrix acts on it by pure scaling. The eigenvalue \(\lambda\) tells the story:

  • \(\lambda > 0\): stretch along \(v\)
  • \(\lambda < 0\): stretch and flip
  • \(|\lambda| > 1\): expansion; \(|\lambda| < 1\): contraction
  • \(\lambda = 0\): collapse to zero
  • Complex \(\lambda\): rotation and scaling combined

A matrix can look complicated, but its eigenvalues summarize what it fundamentally does to space.

As an example, let’s start with a 2×2 matrix where all eigenvalues are positive:

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]

This is a positive definite matrix: symmetric with all positive eigenvalues. Such matrices appear everywhere in machine learning (covariance matrices, kernel matrices, Hessians at minima) because they guarantee convexity and stability.

import numpy as np

# Example: Positive definite matrix
A = np.array([[2, 1], 
              [1, 2]])

# Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(A1)
print(f"Eigenvalues: {eigenvalues}")
print(f"Eigenvectors:\n{eigenvectors}")
Eigenvalues: [3. 1.]
Eigenvectors:
[[ 0.70710678 -0.70710678]
 [ 0.70710678  0.70710678]]

What does this matrix actually do? Each column of \(A\) tells us where a standard basis vector lands: \(e_1 = [1,0]\) maps to \(Ae_1 = [2,1]\) (coral), and \(e_2 = [0,1]\) maps to \(Ae_2 = [1,2]\) (coral). But this doesn’t reveal the structure.

To see the essence, pass a unit circle through \(A\). Every point on the circle is a unit vector; its image shows how \(A\) stretches and rotates space. The circle becomes an ellipse (coral). The eigenvectors (green) are the axes of this ellipse: they point in the directions where \(A\) acts by pure scaling, with no rotation. Along \(v_1\), space stretches by \(\lambda_1 = 3\). Along \(v_2\), it stretches by \(\lambda_2 = 1\).

The eigenvalues and eigenvectors summarize the matrix: two perpendicular directions and how much each stretches.

Code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Unit circle
theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)
circle = np.array([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])

# Transform circle
ellipse = A @ circle

# Standard basis vectors
e1, e2 = np.array([1, 0]), np.array([0, 1])
Ae1, Ae2 = A @ e1, A @ e2

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.plot(circle[0], circle[1], color='steelblue', linestyle='--', label='Unit circle', alpha=0.6)
ax.plot(ellipse[0], ellipse[1], color='coral', linewidth=2, label='Transformed')

# Standard basis
ax.arrow(0, 0, e1[0]*0.95, e1[1], head_width=0.08, color='steelblue')
ax.arrow(0, 0, e2[0], e2[1]*0.95, head_width=0.08, color='steelblue')
ax.text(e1[0]+0.1, e1[1]+0.1, r'$e_1$', fontsize=12, color='steelblue')
ax.text(e2[0]+0.1, e2[1]+0.1, r'$e_2$', fontsize=12, color='steelblue')

# Their images
ax.arrow(0, 0, Ae1[0]*0.95, Ae1[1]*0.95, head_width=0.08, color='coral')
ax.arrow(0, 0, Ae2[0]*0.95, Ae2[1]*0.95, head_width=0.08, color='coral')
ax.text(Ae1[0]+0.1, Ae1[1]+0.1, r'$Ae_1$', fontsize=12, color='coral')
ax.text(Ae2[0]+0.1, Ae2[1]+0.1, r'$Ae_2$', fontsize=12, color='coral')

# Eigenvectors (scaled by eigenvalues)
for i in range(2):
    ev = eigenvectors[:, i] * eigenvalues[i]
    ax.arrow(0, 0, ev[0]*0.95, ev[1]*0.95, head_width=0.08, color='seagreen', linestyle='--')
ax.text(2.2, 2.2, r'$\lambda_1 v_1$', fontsize=12, color='seagreen')
ax.text(-0.9, 0.9, r'$\lambda_2 v_2$', fontsize=12, color='seagreen')

ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(-4, 4)
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3); ax.legend()
ax.set_title(f'Positive definite: λ = {eigenvalues[0]:.1f}, {eigenvalues[1]:.1f}')
plt.show()

When the matrix is rectangular

Now consider a 2×3 matrix:

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]

Can we compute eigenvalues? The eigenvalue equation \(Av = \lambda v\) requires that \(v\) and \(Av\) live in the same space: we subtract them to get \((A - \lambda I)v = 0\). But here \(v \in \mathbb{R}^3\) and \(Av \in \mathbb{R}^2\). The dimensions don’t match. There is no identity matrix \(I\) that makes \(A - \lambda I\) meaningful.

Eigenvalues are fundamentally about a matrix acting on a space and returning to that same space. Rectangular matrices map between different spaces. We need a different tool.

The Four Subspaces of a Matrix

For a square non-singular matrix, eigenvectors live in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and since the matrix is full rank, the row space = column space = \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The null spaces are trivial (just \(\{0\}\)). So there’s only “one space” in play.

For a rectangular \(m \times n\) matrix \(A\), we have two distinct spaces:

  • Input space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) splits into: row space + null space
  • Output space \(\mathbb{R}^m\) splits into: column space + left null space

Now here’s the key:

  • \(A^T A\) is \(n \times n\), symmetric → its eigenvectors live in the input space \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
  • \(AA^T\) is \(m \times m\), symmetric → its eigenvectors live in the output space \(\mathbb{R}^m\)

And the beautiful fact: these eigenvectors don’t just live anywhere in those spaces. They split them:

  • Eigenvectors of \(A^T A\) with nonzero eigenvalues → span the row space
  • Eigenvectors of \(A^T A\) with zero eigenvalues → span the null space

Similarly for \(AA^T\):

  • Eigenvectors of \(AA^T\) with nonzero eigenvalues → span the column space
  • Eigenvectors of \(AA^T\) with zero eigenvalues → span the left null space

And the miracle: \(A^T A\) and \(AA^T\) share the same nonzero eigenvalues. So we get paired bases that are connected through the singular values.

To summarize the SVD picture:

Matrix Space Nonzero eigenvalue eigenvectors Zero eigenvalue eigenvectors
\(A^T A\) Input \(\mathbb{R}^n\) Row space (→ \(v_1, \ldots, v_r\)) Null space (→ \(v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n\))
\(AA^T\) Output \(\mathbb{R}^m\) Column space (→ \(u_1, \ldots, u_r\)) Left null space (→ \(u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_m\))

And the coupling: \(Av_k = \sigma_k u_k\) for \(k \leq r\), while \(Av_k = 0\) for \(k > r\).

SVD: Finding structure in both spaces

The solution is to work with \(A^T A\) and \(AA^T\) instead. Both are square and symmetric, so we can compute their eigenvalues and eigenvectors. And they turn out to be deeply connected.

For our 2×3 matrix \(A\): - \(A^T A\) is 3×3, living in the input space \(\mathbb{R}^3\) - \(AA^T\) is 2×2, living in the output space \(\mathbb{R}^2\)

Their eigenvectors partition these spaces:

Input space \(\mathbb{R}^3\) Output space \(\mathbb{R}^2\)
Where \(A\) acts Row space Column space
What \(A\) kills Null space Left null space

The eigenvectors of \(A^T A\) with nonzero eigenvalues span the row space; those with zero eigenvalues span the null space. Similarly, the eigenvectors of \(AA^T\) split the output space into column space and left null space.

The key fact: \(A^T A\) and \(AA^T\) share the same nonzero eigenvalues. This links the two spaces through the singular values \(\sigma_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k}\).

Variational Formulation

Variational Principle

A variational Principle is defined as a fundamental concept in mathematical physics that aims to determine the path, function, or object that maximizes or minimizes a mathematical quantity known as a functional. It encompasses various principles, such as the principle of least action, which states that a moving system follows the path that minimizes the action integral.
